## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  ----------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module                  Multimodal Generative AI
  Code                    CSC_52002_EP
  Team and workload       Head: Vicky Kalogeiton (École Polytechnique) · head of the X3A session: Xi Wang · course staff: Mohamed Alami Chehboune, Lucas Degeorge, Eleftherios Tsonis, Xi Wang, Yuanzhi Zhu · 36 h (18 h of lectures + 18 h of small-class sessions) · 4.5 ECTS · VAEs, GANs, diffusion, CLIP and text-to-image — how generative models bring together text, images and structured data.
  Period                  Autumn semester · period 2 (from 04/01/2027 to 19/03/2027) · X3A session "Multimodal Generative AI"; course taught in English
  Assessment              Not communicated on the official course description; resit allowed (the final grade is the max of the two grades); the course unit is earned if the final grade ≥ 10
  Status in the program   [Recommended — LLGA track]{.badge .recommended}
  ----------------------- --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: an engineer who knows a CNN / autoencoder and wants to generate or align text×image. **Empirical first**: a VAE that reconstructs blurry (β too low); a GAN that mode-collapses after 20 k steps; a CLIP whose retrieval drops as soon as the domain leaves the web — then we name ELBO, diffusion, guidance.

VAE, GAN, diffusion, CLIP and text-to-image. Bridge to neural rendering and generative control in M2.

### What you will be able to do

-   Derive and train a VAE: ELBO, reparameterization, latent spaces and their properties.
-   Explain adversarial GAN training, its equilibria and instabilities, and the contribution of the Wasserstein variant.
-   Describe generation by diffusion: DDPM and score matching, and the link between the two viewpoints.
-   Use guidance (notably classifier-free), accelerated sampling (DDIM) and latent diffusion.
-   Understand CLIP and the alignment of vision-language spaces that makes text-to-image possible.
-   Assemble the complete text-to-image pipeline and identify the role of each component.
-   Situate the extensions of generation beyond images: video, 3D and multimodal LLMs.
-   Evaluate generative models (notably with FID), estimate their computational costs and discuss their ethical issues.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026-2027 catalog)

The official course description (X3A session "Multimodal Generative AI") starts from the observation that generative AI enables machines "to interpret and process data like humans, via several modalities and sensors: vision, audio, tactile information", and that the rise of multimodal generative AI is "a major scientific breakthrough" as much as "a paradigm shift that reconfigures entire industries, from healthcare to automotive" — citing Dall-E 3, Midjourney and GPT-Vision, which build on large vision models, and the expansion of autonomous driving. Stated objective: "to go beyond CNNs and transformers" and to cover "the advanced topics of multimodal generative AI: from image to video generation, sound and robot actions". Official volume: 36 h (18 h of lectures + 18 h of small-class sessions); course taught in English. Detailed week-by-week syllabus, official prerequisites and assessment modalities: not communicated on the description (resit: max of the two grades; course unit earned if final grade ≥ 10).

  Official topic of the description                                        Course section
  ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Beyond CNNs and transformers: advanced generative families               Chapters 1 to 4 (VAEs, GANs and Wasserstein, DDPM/score diffusion, guidance, DDIM and latent diffusion)
  Large vision models and tools such as Dall-E 3, Midjourney, GPT-Vision   Chapters 5 (CLIP, vision-language alignment) and 6 (the complete text-to-image pipeline)
  From image to video and 3D                                               Chapter 7 (beyond images: video, 3D, LLMs)
  Sound                                                                    Chapter 7 mentions it; full sound processing is referred to the M2 module [Speech Technology for Conversational AI](../m2-speech-technology/index.html)
  Reconfigured industries (healthcare, automotive), autonomous driving     Chapter 8 (evaluation, costs, ethics) as a reading grid

Official topics not covered (honestly flagged): robot actions and tactile data, absent from these materials. Our extensions, beyond the official description: the refresher chapter 0 (probabilities, networks, ELBO) and chapter 9 (the research of the course instructors).

### Where this course fits in the program

Module of period 2 of M1 (36 h, 4.5 ECTS): an option explicitly **recommended for the LLGA track**, of which Vicky Kalogeiton is the official head (the X3A session being led by Xi Wang). Official prerequisites: not communicated on the course description. This is where the master's program shifts from learning representations to multimodal generation.

-   **Prerequisites** — [Deep Learning](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html) for architectures and training (the review section covers probabilities, networks and the ELBO, hence VAEs and GANs); the [Signal Processing](../m1p1-signal-processing/index.html) module is useful for the signal and spectrogram processing mobilized by the audio and video extensions.
-   **Downstream modules** — it directly grounds [Control in Generative AI](../m2-control-generative-ai/index.html) (M2), which teaches how to steer these generative models; it prepares [Advanced Topics in Large Language Models](../m2-advanced-topics-llms/index.html) (M2) for multimodal LLMs, and [Speech Technology for Conversational AI](../m2-speech-technology/index.html) (M2) for speech generation.

### Course outline

-   **Review: probabilities, networks, ELBO** — the probabilistic and neural foundation reactivated before the generative models.
-   **VAEs and latent spaces** — encoding and decoding with a distribution: the first generative building block.
-   **GANs: adversary, equilibrium, Wasserstein** — learning through a game between generator and discriminator.
-   **Diffusion: DDPM and score matching** — denoising progressively: the paradigm that dominates generation.
-   **Guidance, DDIM and latent diffusion** — controlling generation, speeding it up and making it computationally affordable.
-   **CLIP and vision-language alignment** — the common space where text and image meet.
-   **Text-to-image: the complete pipeline** — assembling tokenizer, latent space, diffusion and decoder.
-   **Beyond images: video, 3D, LLMs** — the current frontiers of multimodal generation.
-   **Evaluation, costs, ethics** — measuring quality (FID among others), weighing costs, questioning uses.
-   **Course research notes (Kalogeiton et al.)** — a tour of the research work related to the course.
-   **Exercises** and **References** — systematic training and sources to go further.

### How to study this module

-   Start with the review section and make sure you can derive the ELBO: VAEs, and later latent diffusion, collapse without it.
-   Train a small VAE on a simple dataset before tackling GANs: the contrast between the two ways of learning to generate is very instructive.
-   For each model, write down in black and white the loss function and the sampling algorithm: in generative modeling, these two lines summarize everything.
-   Follow the thread of latent spaces: VAEs, then latent diffusion, then CLIP form a progression, not three independent chapters.
-   Take this module alongside [Machine learning with Optimal Transport and Algorithmic Fairness](../m1p2-optimal-transport/index.html) (same period): the Wasserstein distance, the Wasserstein-GAN and the FID illuminate one another there.
-   Redo the exercises of each section before moving on to the next, and keep the final chapter (evaluation, costs, ethics) as a critical reading grid for everything else.

::: note
[Independent note]{.tag} This module is the multimodal generative component of the master's program: it crosses the LLM track (CLIP and multimodal LLMs) with the mathematical rigor of transport (Wasserstein, FID), and prepares the control of generation in M2 in [Control in Generative AI](../m2-control-generative-ai/index.html). Creative industries, data synthesis, computer-aided design: industrial demand there is immense, and the questions of evaluation, costs and ethics it raises are at the heart of the field's current debates.
:::

## 0. Review: probabilities, networks, ELBO {#ch0}

This module builds the entire edifice of multimodal generative models on four bricks: **Gaussians** (the only probabilistic object diffusion will need), the **evidence lower bound** (ELBO), the **reparameterization trick** (making sampling differentiable) and **encoder-decoder architectures** (CNN, U-Net, attention). We prove them here once and for all: they will be reused in the five following chapters.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Reminders from previous modules
:::

-   **ELBO / VAE** (Deep Learning, ch. 7): $\mathbb{E}_q[\log p_\theta(x\mid z)] - \mathrm{KL}(q_\phi(z\mid x) \| p(z))$; reparameterization trick;
-   **CNN**: convolutions, U-Net (encoder-decoder skip connections);
-   **Transformers & cross-attention**: image queries, text keys/values — the mechanism that "injects" the prompt into a generator;
-   **Gaussians**: additive noise, $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$, reparameterization — diffusion is just a chain of Gaussian noises (Refresher Statistics, chains);
-   **EM / PCA** (Machine Learning module): the VAE is a probabilistic cousin of PCA — alternating maximization of a lower bound, principal axes = latent directions.
::::

::: prop
[Property 0.1 — Sum of independent Gaussians]{.tag} If $X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \sigma_1^2)$ and $Y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_2, \sigma_2^2)$ are independent, then $X + Y \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_1 + \mu_2,\ \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2)$. The means add, *the variances add* — it is this rule that makes diffusion "computable in a single step" (chapter 3).
:::

::: proof
Proof (characteristic function). For $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$, one computes $\varphi_Z(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{itZ}] = e^{i\mu t - \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2 t^2}$ (a Gaussian integral after completing the square). By independence, $\varphi_{X+Y}(t) = \varphi_X(t)\,\varphi_Y(t) = e^{i(\mu_1+\mu_2)t - \frac{1}{2}(\sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)t^2}$, which is the characteristic function of a $\mathcal{N}(\mu_1+\mu_2,\ \sigma_1^2+\sigma_2^2)$; Lévy's uniqueness theorem concludes. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 0.2 — ELBO (Jensen)]{.tag} For every $x$, every proposal distribution $q_\phi(z)$ whose support contains that of $p_\theta(z \mid x)$: $$\log p_\theta(x) \;=\; \mathrm{ELBO}_\phi(x) + \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(z) \,\|\, p_\theta(z\mid x)\big) \;\ge\; \mathrm{ELBO}_\phi(x),$$ $$\mathrm{ELBO}_\phi(x) = \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}\big[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)\big] - \mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(z\mid x)\,\|\,p(z)\big).$$ The gap between $\log p_\theta(x)$ and the bound is exactly the KL: maximizing the ELBO brings $q_\phi$ closer to the true posterior *and* maximizes the likelihood.
:::

::: proof
We write the integral as an expectation under $q_\phi$, then apply the concavity of the logarithm (Jensen's inequality: $\log \mathbb{E}[U] \ge \mathbb{E}[\log U]$): $$\log p_\theta(x) = \log \int p_\theta(x\mid z)\, p(z)\, dz = \log \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}\!\left[\frac{p_\theta(x\mid z)\,p(z)}{q_\phi(z\mid x)}\right] \ge \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}\!\left[\log \frac{p_\theta(x\mid z)\,p(z)}{q_\phi(z\mid x)}\right] = \mathrm{ELBO}_\phi(x).$$ Moreover $\log \frac{p_\theta(x\mid z)p(z)}{q_\phi(z)} = \log p_\theta(x) + \log\frac{p_\theta(z\mid x)}{q_\phi(z)}$; taking the expectation under $q_\phi$, the second term becomes $-\mathrm{KL}(q_\phi \| p_\theta(z\mid x))$, hence the exact decomposition. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: def
[Definition 0.3 — Reparameterization trick]{.tag} Sampling $z \sim q_\phi(z\mid x) = \mathcal{N}(\mu_\phi(x), \mathrm{diag}\,\sigma_\phi^2(x))$ blocks the gradient ($\nabla_\phi$ of a random draw). Instead we write $$z = \mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x) \odot \epsilon, \qquad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I),$$ so that $\nabla_\phi\, \mathbb{E}_{q_\phi}[f_\phi(z)] = \mathbb{E}_{\epsilon}\big[\nabla_\phi f_\phi(\mu_\phi(x) + \sigma_\phi(x)\odot\epsilon)\big]$: the noise distribution no longer depends on $\phi$, and the gradient passes *under* the expectation. The same trick will make diffusion differentiable end to end.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 0.4 — KL between diagonal Gaussians (closed form)]{.tag} For $q = \mathcal{N}(\mu_1, \mathrm{diag}\,\sigma_1^2)$ and $p = \mathcal{N}(\mu_2, \mathrm{diag}\,\sigma_2^2)$: $$\mathrm{KL}(q \| p) = \tfrac{1}{2}\sum_i \left[\frac{\sigma_{1,i}^2 + (\mu_{1,i}-\mu_{2,i})^2}{\sigma_{2,i}^2} + \log\frac{\sigma_{2,i}^2}{\sigma_{1,i}^2} - 1\right].$$ All of VAE training (and of diffusion, ch. 3) rests on the fact that this quantity is evaluated *in closed form*. The proof (a direct expectation computation) is the subject of exercise 3, with solution.
:::

**Networks.** A *CNN* applies the same filter locally; its receptive field grows with depth, trading resolution for context. The **U-Net** couples an encoder (downsampling, global semantics) and a decoder (upsampling, local precision) through *skip connections* that short-circuit the bottleneck: it is the reference denoising architecture for diffusion. **Cross-attention** injects the text: $$\mathrm{Attn}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d}}\right)V, \qquad Q = W_Q\,h_{\text{image}}, \quad K = W_K\, e_{\text{text}}, \quad V = W_V\, e_{\text{text}},$$ where $h_{\text{image}}$ are the spatial activations of the denoiser and $e_{\text{text}}$ the tokens of the prompt: every image position "queries" the text (cf. Deep Learning module, ch. 6).

  Family           Learning                   Strengths                          Weaknesses
  ---------------- -------------------------- ---------------------------------- ---------------------------
  VAE              likelihood (ELBO)          structured latent, fast            blurry, loose ELBO
  GAN              adversarial                sharp, realistic                   unstable, lost modes
  Diffusion        denoising (score)          SOTA quality/diversity, guidance   slow (multi-step), costly
  Autoregressive   sequential cross-entropy   exact probabilistic                slow sequential

## 1. VAEs and latent spaces {#ch1}

Concrete scene: text-to-image on a product brief. CFG too high → saturated OOD images; too low → the prompt is ignored. This chapter fixes generative objectives before architectures.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Posterior collapse (VAE); mode collapse (GAN); miscalibrated guidance (diffusion); evaluating only FID while missing semantic failures.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Conditional & hierarchical VAE]{.tag} Conditioning the generation: $p_\theta(x \mid c)$ with $c$ a class, a text (encoded), another modality. **Hierarchical VAEs** (HiVAE) stack latents $p(z_1 \mid z_2)\, p(z_2 \mid z_3)\dots$; **VQ-VAEs** quantize the latent into a learned dictionary (discrete codes — the ancestor of image tokens); VQ-VAE-2 reached image fidelity before diffusion.
:::

::: prop
[What the latent buys]{.tag} Compressing $512 \times 512 \times 3$ into $64 \times 64$ latents = $\times 64$ less computation; all large image generative models (Stable Diffusion, DALL·E 2/3) generate in latent space — the autoencoder (light) and the generator (heavy) are decoupled. The same principle applies to *graphs*: latent graph, discrete codes (Graph ML module, ch. 7).
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 1.2 — ELBO decomposition: reconstruction + regularization]{.tag} $$\mathrm{ELBO}_\phi(x) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z\mid x)}\big[\log p_\theta(x \mid z)\big]}_{\text{reconstruction}} \;-\; \underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\big(q_\phi(z\mid x)\,\|\,p(z)\big)}_{\text{latent regularization}}.$$ *Interpretation of the two forces*: the first term asks for a $z$ that *explains* $x$ (auto-encoding), the second for a $z$ that is *typical* under the prior. The tension between the two structures the latent space: without the KL, $q$ can memorize ("hole" regions not covered by the prior); without reconstruction, $z$ encodes nothing.
:::

::: proof
The decomposition is already the form obtained in thm. 0.2; what matters is seeing where each term comes from. Expand $\mathbb{E}_{q}\big[\log \frac{p_\theta(x\mid z)\,p(z)}{q_\phi(z\mid x)}\big]$: $$\mathbb{E}_q[\log p_\theta(x\mid z)] + \mathbb{E}_q[\log p(z)] - \mathbb{E}_q[\log q_\phi(z\mid x)] = \mathbb{E}_q[\log p_\theta(x\mid z)] - \mathrm{KL}(q_\phi \| p),$$ where we recognize the definition $\mathrm{KL}(q\|p) = \mathbb{E}_q[\log q - \log p]$. When $p_\theta(x\mid z)$ is a diagonal Gaussian of mean $D_\theta(z)$ and fixed variance $\sigma^2$, the reconstruction term equals $-\frac{1}{2\sigma^2}\|x - D_\theta(z)\|^2 + \mathrm{cst}$: the "reconstruction MSE" of the labs is nothing but the negative of a Gaussian log-likelihood. When $q_\phi$ and $p$ are Gaussian, the second term closes via prop. 0.4. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: note
[Posterior collapse: diagnosis and remedies]{.tag} The decoder (often an autoregressive transformer) becomes so powerful that it ignores $z$: $q_\phi(z\mid x) \to p(z)$, the KL drops toward 0 and the VAE degenerates into a non-conditional model (the latent "collapses"). Causes: a strong autoregressive decoder, a dominant KL early in training, an overly simple prior.

-   **KL annealing**: weight the KL by a coefficient that slowly rises from 0 to 1 — let the reconstruction settle first;
-   **$\beta$-VAE** (Higgins et al., 2017): maximizing $\mathbb{E}[\log p(x\mid z)] - \beta\,\mathrm{KL}$ with $\beta > 1$ forces a *disentangled* latent (one direction = one factor of variation); in practice, against collapse one rather uses $\beta < 1$;
-   **Free bits**: penalize the KL *per dimension* only beyond a budget $\lambda$: $\max(\mathrm{KL}_j, \lambda)$ — every dimension receives a free "information allowance", which prevents it from dying.
:::

::: thm
[Construction 1.3 — VQ-VAE: quantizing the latent]{.tag} The encoder produces $z_e(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times D}$; a *codebook* $\{e_1, \dots, e_K\} \subset \mathbb{R}^D$ is learned; each position is quantized to the nearest code: $$z_q(x) = e_k, \qquad k = \arg\min_j \|z_e(x) - e_j\|_2.$$ The argmin is not differentiable. One uses the **straight-through** estimator (gradient copy) and the total loss: $$\mathcal{L} = \log p_\theta\big(x \mid z_q\big) + \big\|\mathrm{sg}[z_e] - e\big\|_2^2 + \beta\,\big\|z_e - \mathrm{sg}[e]\big\|_2^2,$$ where $\mathrm{sg}$ is the *stop-gradient* operator.
:::

::: proof
Why this three-term loss? **(i)** The reconstruction must be a function of the quantized codes $z_q$ — but $\nabla_{z_e} z_q = 0$ (argmin): we define $\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z_e} \mathrel{:=} \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial z_q}$ (straight-through); the estimator is biased yet empirically effective. **(ii)** The term $\|\mathrm{sg}[z_e] - e\|^2$ is quadratic in $e$ (the codes migrate toward the produced encodings); the stop-gradient symmetrically prevents the encoder from moving. **(iii)** The term $\beta\|z_e - \mathrm{sg}[e]\|^2$ does the opposite: it pulls the encoder toward the codes. The two "gear" (commitment) terms synchronize encoder and dictionary, while the first term trains the decoder; together they implement a continuous K-means inside the training loop. [∎]{.qed}
:::

**Hierarchy and sampling.** In a HiVAE, the ELBO becomes $$\mathbb{E}_{q(z_1, z_2\mid x)}\big[\log p_\theta(x \mid z_1) + \log p(z_1 \mid z_2) + \log p(z_2) - \log q_\phi(z_1 \mid x, z_2) - \log q_\phi(z_2 \mid x)\big],$$ each level compressing the previous one (the "low" scales govern composition, the "high" ones the details — exactly the levels of a U-Net). To *generate*: sample $z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$ (or the levels of the learned prior, as in VQ-VAE-2), then decode in a single network pass; *latent traversals* (interpolating $z$ between two images) are the visual test of the continuity of the learned space.

```python
import torch

class MiniVAE(torch.nn.Module):
    """Minimal convolutional VAE for MNIST-like data (28x28)."""
    def __init__(self, d=8):
        super().__init__()
        self.enc = torch.nn.Sequential(            # x: (B,1,28,28)
            torch.nn.Conv2d(1, 32, 4, 2, 1), torch.nn.ReLU(),   # 14x14
            torch.nn.Conv2d(32, 64, 4, 2, 1), torch.nn.ReLU(),  # 7x7
            torch.nn.Flatten(), torch.nn.Linear(64*7*7, 2*d))
        self.dec = torch.nn.Sequential(
            torch.nn.Linear(d, 64*7*7), torch.nn.Unflatten(1, (64, 7, 7)),
            torch.nn.ConvTranspose2d(64, 32, 4, 2, 1), torch.nn.ReLU(),
            torch.nn.ConvTranspose2d(32, 1, 4, 2, 1), torch.nn.Sigmoid())
    def forward(self, x):
        h = self.enc(x); mu, logvar = h.chunk(2, dim=1)
        z = mu + torch.exp(0.5*logvar) * torch.randn_like(mu)   # reparametrization
        return self.dec(z), mu, logvar

def vae_loss(x, xh, mu, logvar, beta=1.0):
    rec = torch.nn.functional.binary_cross_entropy(
        xh, x, reduction="sum") / x.size(0)                      # reconstruction
    kl  = -0.5 * torch.sum(1 + logvar - mu.pow(2) - logvar.exp()) / x.size(0)
    return rec + beta * kl                                      # ELBO (prop. 0.4)
```

::: note
[LLGA analogies]{.tag} The VQ-VAE manufactures *image tokens*: DALL·E 1 generates these tokens autoregressively (LLMs module), latent diffusion replaces them with continuous denoising (ch. 4). On graphs, the same discrete/continuous dichotomy opposes discrete VAEs and edge diffusion (Graph ML, ch. 7); in NLP, the CLIP "latent" (ch. 5) is the shared text-image space.
:::

## 2. GANs: adversary, equilibrium, Wasserstein {#ch2}

::: def
[Definition 2.1 — The minimax game and its refinements]{.tag} $$\min_G \max_D\ V(D, G) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\mathrm{data}}}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p(z)}[\log(1 - D(G(z)))]$$ $D$ classifies "real/fake", $G$ forges counterfeits. In practice one uses the *non-saturated* form $\max_G \mathbb{E}_z[\log D(G(z))]$ (same equilibria, stronger gradients early in training), or alternative losses: *least-squares GAN*, *hinge*. **Conditional** version: $G(z, c)$, $D(x, c)$ — Pix2Pix (image-to-image with an L1 reconstruction constraint).
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 2.2 — Equilibrium of the game]{.tag}

1.  For fixed $G$, the optimal discriminator is $$D^\*(x) = \frac{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)}{p_{\mathrm{data}}(x) + p_g(x)}.$$
2.  At this $D^\*$, $V(G^\*) = -\log 4 + 2\,\mathrm{JS}(p_{\mathrm{data}} \| p_g)$; the global minimum is attained only for $p_g = p_{\mathrm{data}}$: *at equilibrium, the generator exactly reproduces the data distribution*.
:::

::: proof
**(i)** The problem separates pointwise: for each $x$, maximize $u(D) = p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)\log D + p_g(x)\log(1-D)$ over $D \in (0,1)$. The derivative $u'(D) = \frac{p_{\mathrm{data}}}{D} - \frac{p_g}{1-D}$ vanishes at $D^\* = \frac{p_{\mathrm{data}}}{p_{\mathrm{data}} + p_g}$ (a maximum, since $u \to -\infty$ at the boundaries). **(ii)** Substituting: $V(D^\*) = p\log\frac{p}{p+q} + q\log\frac{q}{p+q}$. Subtracting and adding $(p+q)\log\frac{1}{2}$, we obtain $$V(D^\*) = -\log 4 + \Big[p\log\frac{2p}{p+q} + q\log\frac{2q}{p+q}\Big] = -\log 4 + 2\,\mathrm{JS}(p\|q),$$ where $\mathrm{JS}(p\|q) = \tfrac12\mathrm{KL}(p\|\tfrac{p+q}{2}) + \tfrac12\mathrm{KL}(q\|\tfrac{p+q}{2})$ (definition; it is a KL toward a probability law, hence always finite). Since $\mathrm{JS} \ge 0$ with equality iff $p = q$, the minimax value is $-\log 4$, attained only when the generator matches the target law. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: ex
[Example 2.3 — The Gaussian case]{.tag} If $p_{\mathrm{data}} = \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ and $p_g = \mathcal{N}(\mu_g, \sigma_g^2)$, formula (i) gives an explicit $D^\*$ (via the densities): the optimal classifier is a sigmoid of a quadratic score — two Gaussians separate along a quadratic boundary. Backpropagating $\log D^\*(G(z))$ pushes $\mu_g \to \mu$ and $\sigma_g^2 \to \sigma^2$: this is the toy version (exercise 4) of the theorem.
:::

::: note
[Mode collapse: analysis and mitigations]{.tag} The theorem describes the *global* equilibrium, but the game is non-cooperative: $G$ may find it profitable to produce in a loop *one* highly deceptive image (one mode of the distribution), then switch to another — oscillations and loss of diversity. The gradient of $G$ only "sees" the generated points: never-sampled modes are never corrected. Mitigations:

-   **Minibatch discrimination**: for each $x_i$ of the batch, add to $D$ intra-batch similarity features $o(x_i) = \sum_{j \ne i} \exp\!\big(-\|f(x_i) - f(x_j)\|\big)\,T_{ij}$ — the discriminator detects "all-identical" batches;
-   **Unrolled GAN**: $G$ is trained against the $D$ it *will face* (k lookahead steps of the discriminator), which removes pure pursuit cycles;
-   **LLGA monitoring**: intra-batch diversity (mean LPIPS), FID on large cohorts — the industrial diagnostics of ch. 8.
:::

::: thm
[Construction 2.4 — WGAN: Wasserstein to the rescue of JS]{.tag} When the supports of $p$ and $q$ are disjoint or "nearly" so, JS is constant (value $\log 2$) and its gradient vanishes: no more learning signal. The Wasserstein distance $W_1$, on the other hand, stays informative. By the Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality (OT module): $$W_1(p, q) = \sup_{\|f\|_L \le 1}\ \mathbb{E}_{p}[f(x)] - \mathbb{E}_{q}[f(x)],$$ hence the adversarial learning $\min_G \max_{\|D\|_L \le 1} \mathbb{E}_{p}[D] - \mathbb{E}_{q}[D]$: $D$ becomes a 1-Lipschitz *critic*, and the loss is continuous in the parameters of $G$ even at disjoint supports.
:::

::: proof
Sketch of the duality: for every 1-Lipschitz $f$, $\mathbb{E}_p[f] - \mathbb{E}_q[f] \le \mathbb{E}_{\gamma}[\|x - y\|] \le W_1$ (coupling $\gamma$), hence $\sup \le W_1$; the hard part (the equality, attained by an optimal Kantorovich potential) belongs to the Lagrangian duality of transport — outside the syllabus, see the OT module. **The Lipschitz constraint in practice: gradient penalty.** Weight clipping (original WGAN) enforces Lipschitzness too brutally. Instead we penalize the deviation of the gradient norm from 1 *on interpolations* $\tilde x = \epsilon x + (1-\epsilon)\hat x$ between data $x$ and generation $\hat x$: $$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{GP}} = \lambda\,\big(\|\nabla_{\tilde x} D(\tilde x)\|_2 - 1\big)^2.$$ Why $(\|\nabla D\| - 1)^2$ and not $\max(0, \|\nabla D\| - 1)$: penalizing *too-small* gradients as well prevents $D$ from flattening out (loss of signal); why interpolations: the supremum of the dual "lives" along the transport segments between the two distributions — that is where the constraint matters. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: thm
[Architecture 2.5 — StyleGAN: from noise to style]{.tag}

1.  **Mapping network**: $w = m(z)$, an 8-layer MLP — $w$ lives in a "disentangled" space where directions correspond to attributes;
2.  **AdaIN (adaptive instance norm)**: at each generator layer, the style modulates the instance normalization: $$\mathrm{AdaIN}(x, w) = \sigma(w_s)\,\frac{x - \mu(x)}{\sigma(x)} + w_b,$$ where $(w_s, w_b)$ are affine transformations of $w$ specific to the layer — each resolution receives its own style;
3.  **Style mixing**: during training, inject two different $w$ depending on the layers (one for coarse resolutions, the other for fine ones) — this regularizes the mapping and uncovers the structure/texture hierarchy;
4.  **Truncation trick**: at generation, $w' = \bar w + \psi\,(w - \bar w)$ with $\psi < 1$, $\bar w$ the mapping mean — one stays in the high densities: higher fidelity, reduced diversity (exercise 10).
:::

::: prop
[CycleGAN: cycle consistency, proved useful]{.tag} Without training pairs, translate $X \to Y$ with $G$ and $Y \to X$ with $F$ using $$\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cyc}} = \mathbb{E}_x\big[\|F(G(x)) - x\|_1\big] + \mathbb{E}_y\big[\|G(F(y)) - y\|_1\big].$$ *Why this is the right constraint.* The adversarial loss alone allows $G(x) = y_0$ for every $x$ (a single highly "realistic" image fools $D$: cross-domain collapse, and the content of $x$ is lost). If $F(G(x)) = x$ for every $x$ in the support, then $G$ is injective: it can neither collapse modes nor destroy content information — it can only change what $F$ knows how to restore. Cycle consistency is an *information-preserving* constraint made differentiable; combined with the adversarial loss (which imposes the target-domain style), it achieves the translation. The L1 term (rather than L2) favors sharpness (less blurry averaging).
:::

::: note
[Evaluation: IS and FID]{.tag} **Inception Score**: $\mathrm{IS} = \exp\big(\mathbb{E}_x\,\mathrm{KL}(\,p(y\mid x)\,\|\,p(y)\,)\big)$ — each image must be clearly classifiable ($p(y\|x)$ peaked) and the whole set diverse ($p(y)$ spread). **FID**: fit a Gaussian to the Inception features of the real images $(\mu_r, \Sigma_r)$ and of the generated ones $(\mu_g, \Sigma_g)$, then $$\mathrm{FID} = \|\mu_r - \mu_g\|^2 + \mathrm{tr}\big(\Sigma_r + \Sigma_g - 2(\Sigma_r\Sigma_g)^{1/2}\big) \;=\; W_2^2\ \text{(Bures) between the two Gaussians}$$ — a direct application of the Wasserstein-Bures distance of the OT module; analysis of sampling biases in ch. 8. **Why diffusion eventually dominated**: stable loss (a simple denoising MSE), no equilibrium to maintain, natural diversity — but GANs remain unbeatable in speed (1 step) and live on in super-resolution and editing.
:::

## 3. Diffusion: DDPM and score matching {#ch3}

::: thm
[Model 3.1 — Forward process (noising)]{.tag} A Markov chain that adds Gaussian noise: $$q(x_t \mid x_{t-1}) = \mathcal{N}\big(\sqrt{1 - \beta_t}\, x_{t-1},\ \beta_t I\big), \qquad t = 1, \dots, T,$$ with increasing $\beta_t$. Key property (composition of Gaussians): $$q(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\, x_0,\ (1 - \bar\alpha_t) I\big), \qquad \alpha_t = 1 - \beta_t,\quad \bar\alpha_t = \prod_{s = 1}^{t}\alpha_s.$$ For $T = 1000$, $\bar\alpha_T \approx 0$: the image has become pure noise.
:::

::: proof
By induction on $t$. **Base case**: $t = 1$: $x_1 = \sqrt{\alpha_1}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \alpha_1}\,\epsilon$, so $q(x_1 \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_1}x_0,\ (1-\bar\alpha_1)I)$ by definition. **Inductive step**: assume $x_{t-1} \mid x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,x_0,\ (1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})I)$. Then $$x_t = \sqrt{\alpha_t}\,x_{t-1} + \sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\,\epsilon, \qquad \epsilon \perp x_{t-1} \mid x_0.$$ By property 0.1 (sum of *independent* Gaussians): mean $\sqrt{\alpha_t}\cdot\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,x_0 = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0$ (since $\alpha_t \bar\alpha_{t-1} = \bar\alpha_t$); variance $\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}) + (1-\alpha_t) = 1 - \bar\alpha_{t-1} + \alpha_t\bar\alpha_{t-1} = 1 - \bar\alpha_t$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: note
[Variance schedule: linear or cosine]{.tag} The choice of the $\beta_t$ sets the speed of destruction. Linear ($\beta_t: 10^{-4} \to 0.02$, original DDPM): high frequencies die too fast, and the end of the chain is needlessly noisy. **Cosine** (Nichol & Dhariwal, 2021): $$\bar\alpha_t = \frac{f(t)}{f(0)}, \qquad f(t) = \cos^2\!\left(\frac{t/T + 0.008}{1.008}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}\right),$$ which gives a gently sloped decay of $\bar\alpha_t$, effective also at low resolution. Rule of thumb: the schedule must destroy information *uniformly* across the scales of the image.
:::

::: thm
[Model 3.2 — Learned reverse process and per-step ELBO]{.tag} $$p_\theta(x_{t-1} \mid x_t) = \mathcal{N}\big(\mu_\theta(x_t, t),\ \sigma_t^2 I\big), \qquad p(x_T) = \mathcal{N}(0, I),$$ and training reduces to **a simple MSE**: $$\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_{x_0, \epsilon, t}\big[\|\epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\|^2\big], \qquad x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon.$$
:::

::: proof
**Step 1 — telescoping.** Applying thm. 0.2 to the chain $p_\theta(x_{0:T})$ with $q(x_{1:T}\mid x_0)$, the ELBO rewrites (Markov chain, telescoped products): $$-\mathrm{ELBO} = \mathrm{KL}\big(q(x_T\mid x_0)\,\|\,\mathcal{N}(0,I)\big) + \sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_q\!\left[\mathrm{KL}\big(q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t, x_0)\,\|\,p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\big)\right] = L_T + \sum_t L_{t-1}.$$ **Step 2 — closed-form forward posterior.** By Bayes' rule $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t, x_0) \propto q(x_t \mid x_{t-1})\,q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0)$: a product of two Gaussians in $x_{t-1}$, hence Gaussian; completing the square: $$q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t, x_0) = \mathcal{N}\big(\tilde\mu_t(x_t, x_0),\ \tilde\beta_t I\big), \quad \tilde\beta_t = \frac{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\beta_t,\quad \tilde\mu_t = \frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,\beta_t}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \frac{\sqrt{\alpha_t}(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,x_t.$$ **Step 3 — every $L_{t-1}$ is a KL of Gaussians**: closed by prop. 0.4. If we set $\sigma_t^2 = \tilde\beta_t$, what remains is to align the means: $L_{t-1} = C + \frac{1}{2\sigma_t^2}\|\tilde\mu_t - \mu_\theta\|^2$. **Step 4 — noise parameterization.** We choose $$\mu_\theta(x_t, t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Big(x_t - \frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\,\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\Big),$$ which amounts (substituting $x_0 = (x_t - \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon)/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$ into $\tilde\mu_t$) to requiring $\epsilon_\theta \approx \epsilon$; all the remaining factors are known constants absorbed into the weighting. Hence the single MSE of model 3.2 — a remarkable result: *five lines of theory for a one-line loss*. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 3.3 — Predicting the noise = predicting the score]{.tag} $$\epsilon = -\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\;\nabla_{x_t}\log p(x_t \mid x_0).$$ The denoising MSE is therefore a conditional *score matching*: the network learns $\nabla_x \log p$ — exactly the object of the "score-based" family of Song et al. (2021), which unifies diffusion and SDEs (ch. 4).
:::

::: proof
For a Gaussian density $p(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}(x_t;\ m, s^2 I)$ with $m = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0$, $s^2 = 1 - \bar\alpha_t$, we compute $$\nabla_{x_t}\log p(x_t\mid x_0) = \nabla_{x_t}\left[-\frac{\|x_t - m\|^2}{2s^2}\right] + 0 = -\frac{x_t - \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0}{1-\bar\alpha_t}.$$ Now $x_t - \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 = \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon$, so $\nabla_{x_t}\log p = -\epsilon/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}$, that is $\epsilon = -\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\nabla_{x_t}\log p(x_t \mid x_0)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

```python
import torch

def forward_diffusion(x0, t, alphas_bar, eps=None):
    """x_t = sqrt(a_bar_t) x0 + sqrt(1 - a_bar_t) * eps   (in one step!)"""
    if eps is None: eps = torch.randn_like(x0)
    return alphas_bar[t].sqrt()[:, None, None, None] * x0 \
         + (1 - alphas_bar[t]).sqrt()[:, None, None, None] * eps, eps

# Training (typical DDPM loop):
# x0 = batch of images; t ~ U{1..T}
xt, eps = forward_diffusion(x0, t, alphas_bar)
loss = torch.nn.functional.mse_loss(unet(xt, t), eps)   # predict the noise
loss.backward()

# Sampling (T steps, formula of model 3.2):
x = torch.randn(n, c, h, w)                    # x_T ~ N(0, I)
for t in reversed(range(T)):
    eps = unet(x, t)
    mu = (x - beta[t].sqrt()/(1 - alphas_bar[t]).sqrt() * eps) / alpha[t].sqrt()
    x = mu + beta[t].sqrt() * torch.randn_like(x) if t > 0 else mu
```

::: note
[LLGA analogies]{.tag} The diffusion U-Net uses *self-attention* (a transformer on a grid); DiTs replace everything with transformers on patches; and *diffusion on graphs* (DiGress) noises/denoises node and edge types — the same algorithm, another space (Graph ML module, ch. 7). The derivation "Markov chain → ELBO → per-step KL → MSE" we have just done is *literally the same* as the one in Deep Learning module ch. 7 for the VAE — diffusion is a VAE of depth $T$ with shared parameters.
:::

## 4. Guidance, DDIM and latent diffusion {#ch4}

::: thm
[Classifier guidance (Dhariwal & Nichol, 2021)]{.tag} By Bayes, $\log p(x_t \mid y) = \log p(y \mid x_t) + \log p(x_t) - \log p(y)$; taking the gradient in $x_t$, the last term disappears: $$\nabla_{x_t}\log p(x_t \mid y) = \nabla_{x_t}\log p(x_t) + \nabla_{x_t}\log p(y\mid x_t).$$ Via thm. 3.3 ($\epsilon \leftrightarrow -\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\nabla\log p$), the guided denoiser is $$\tilde\epsilon = \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t) - \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\nabla_{x_t}\log p_\psi(y \mid x_t),$$ where $p_\psi$ is a classifier trained on the noised $x_t$. Powerful but costly: a classifier must be trained and evaluated at every step.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 4.1 — Classifier-free guidance (CFG) as a combined direction]{.tag} Train $\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, c)$ with $c$ sometimes replaced by $\varnothing$ (condition dropout, \~10 %); at generation, *extrapolate* the conditional direction: $$\tilde\epsilon = \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, \varnothing) + w\big(\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, c) - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, \varnothing)\big), \qquad w > 1.$$ *Exact interpretation*: $\tilde\epsilon$ is (up to the constant $\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}$) the score of the unnormalized distribution $$p_w(x_t \mid c) \;\propto\; p(x_t \mid c)^{w}\, p(x_t)^{1-w}.$$
:::

::: proof
Again by Bayes, $\nabla\log p(x_t\mid c) = \nabla\log p(c \mid x_t) + \nabla\log p(x_t)$ (the term $\log p(c)$ is constant in $x_t$). The score of $p_w$ is therefore $$\nabla\log p_w = w\,\nabla\log p(x_t\mid c) + (1-w)\,\nabla\log p(x_t) = \nabla\log p(x_t) + w\big(\nabla\log p(x_t\mid c) - \nabla\log p(x_t)\big).$$ Replacing each score by the corresponding denoiser (thm. 3.3), we obtain exactly the CFG rule: it combines *unconditional score + $w$ times the difference of the scores*. For $w = 1$ we recover the conditional score; for $w = 0$ the unconditional one; for $w > 1$, the effective distribution $p(x_t\mid c)^w p(x_t)^{1-w}$ over-weights the conditioning: it is more "peaked" (higher fidelity, better prompt-following) and less diverse. This is the "creativity" slider of all text-to-image tools — and a research topic in its own right (cf. ch. 9, schedules $w(t)$). [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: thm
[Construction 4.2 — DDIM: deriving a family of samplers]{.tag} DDPM fixes $p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)$ as a Gaussian *Markov* kernel. The DDIM trick: any process whose *marginals* $q(x_t \mid x_0)$ are those of model 3.1 and whose expectation is written as a function of $\hat x_0$ leads to the same loss. We posit the non-Markovian family (parameterized by $\sigma_t$): $$q_\sigma(x_{t-1}\mid x_t, x_0) = \mathcal{N}\big(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}-\sigma_t^2}\;\tfrac{x_t - \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}},\ \sigma_t^2 I\big).$$

-   $\sigma_t = \sqrt{\tilde\beta_t}$ recovers **DDPM** (the original Markov process);
-   $\sigma_t = 0$ gives **deterministic DDIM**: same initial noise $x_T$ ⇒ same image (editing via a shared trajectory, reproducible seed);
-   the marginals $q(x_t\mid x_0)$ are unchanged ⇒ the training loss ($\epsilon$-MSE) is *identical*; only the sampler changes;
-   **Step skipping**: since the trajectory is deterministic, one can subsample $\tau_1 < \tau_2 < \dots$ — 20 to 50 steps instead of 1000.
:::

::: proof
Let us check the consistency of the marginals. From $x_{t-1}\mid x_0 \sim \mathcal{N}(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}x_0,\ (1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})I)$ and the definition above, the proposed mean reads $a\,x_0 + b\,(x_t - \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0)$ with $b = \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}-\sigma_t^2}/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}$; conditionally on $x_0$, $x_t$ is Gaussian centered at $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0$, so the mean of $x_{t-1}$ is indeed $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\,x_0$ and its variance $b^2(1-\bar\alpha_t) + \sigma_t^2 = 1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}$ — the desired marginal. We thus obtain infinitely many samplers compatible with the same trained $\epsilon_\theta$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: note
[The SDE viewpoint (Song et al., 2021)]{.tag} As $T \to \infty$, the forward process converges to the SDE $dx = f(x, t)\,dt + g(t)\,dw$. Then *every* SDE has a deterministic companion with the same marginal laws, the **probability flow ODE**: $$\frac{dx}{dt} = f(x, t) - \tfrac{1}{2}g(t)^2\,\nabla_x \log p_t(x).$$ Generating = integrating this ODE backward: this is the theoretical bridge between DDIM (deterministic) and the fast solvers below.
:::

-   **Fast solvers**: DPM-Solver handles the prob-flow ODE by separating the *linear* part (exactly integrable: it is a noised Brownian motion) from the *non-linear* part (the score): "integrating exponential" schemes at 10–15 steps; distillation (consistent models, LCM, adversarial distillation — cf. ch. 9, Di[M]o) targets 1 to 4 steps; quantization (fp16, fp8) compresses the compute — a panorama revisited in M2 ML Ops;
-   **Latent diffusion (Rombach et al., 2022)**: an autoencoder (VQ or KL, ch. 1) compressing the image by a factor 4–8 per side, then diffusion *in the latent*; the denoiser (U-Net or DiT) receives the prompt via cross-attention (def. 0.3) at the levels of maximum resolution; CLIP text encoder: this is the Stable Diffusion architecture;
-   **ControlNet (Zhang et al., 2023)**: conditioning by edges/depth/pose. One copies the blocks of the frozen U-Net encoder ("locked" weights $\theta_{\mathrm{lock}}$), trains a clone $\theta_c$ fed by the conditioning map $c$, and reinjects $$y_c = \mathrm{ZeroConv}_c\big(\mathcal{F}(\cdot;\theta_c)\ +\ \mathcal{F}(x;\theta_{\mathrm{lock}})\big), \qquad y = y_{\mathrm{base}} + y_c,$$ where the *zero-convolutions* (1×1 convolutions initialized to zero) guarantee that at step 0, $y_c = 0$: ControlNet starts as the unchanged model and learns *only* the correction — the same "identity start" trick as zero residuals;
-   **Inpainting / img2img**: noise the starting image up to a step $t_0$ (img2img: $t_0$ tunes fidelity to the start; strong = freedom), then denoise while imposing at every step $x_t = m\odot x_t^{\mathrm{generated}} + (1-m)\odot x_t^{\mathrm{noised}}$ where $m$ is the mask (the RePaint mixing rule; variants relax it at the end of the chain).

::: prop
[DiT: when the transformer replaces the U-Net]{.tag} The latent image is cut into $2\times2$ patches that are "tokenized" (like a ViT); each block = self-attention over the patches + MLP, *modulated by time and condition* via adaLN-Zero: $$h \leftarrow h + \alpha_1\,\mathrm{Attn}\big(\gamma_1 h + \beta_1\big), \qquad h \leftarrow h + \alpha_2\,\mathrm{MLP}\big(\gamma_2 h + \beta_2\big),$$ where $(\gamma, \beta, \alpha)$ are affine functions of $t_{\mathrm{emb}} + c_{\mathrm{emb}}$ and the $\alpha$ are initialized to zero (every block starts as the identity). Quality grows steadily with depth, width and the number of tokens — a "scaling law" behavior typical of transformers, and the basis of modern video generators (ch. 7).
:::

```python
# Minimal DiT: a block modulated by time (adaLN-Zero)
class DiTBlock(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, n_heads):
        super().__init__()
        self.norm1 = torch.nn.LayerNorm(d, elementwise_affine=False)
        self.attn  = torch.nn.MultiheadAttention(d, n_heads, batch_first=True)
        self.norm2 = torch.nn.LayerNorm(d, elementwise_affine=False)
        self.mlp   = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(d, 4*d), torch.nn.GELU(),
                                         torch.nn.Linear(4*d, d))
        self.mod = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.SiLU(), torch.nn.Linear(d, 6*d))
        for m in [self.mod[-1]]:        # zero-init of the alphas
            torch.nn.init.zeros_(m.weight); torch.nn.init.zeros_(m.bias)
    def forward(self, h, cond):                     # h: (B, N, d) patches
        g1, b1, a1, g2, b2, a2 = self.mod(cond).unsqueeze(1).chunk(6, dim=-1)
        h = h + a1 * self.attn(self.norm1(h)*g1 + b1, self.norm1(h)*g1 + b1,
                               self.norm1(h)*g1 + b1)[0]
        return h + a2 * self.mlp(self.norm2(h)*g2 + b2)
```

## 5. CLIP and vision-language alignment {#ch5}

::: thm
[CLIP (Radford et al., 2021)]{.tag} Encode images and texts *jointly* in a shared space: an image encoder (ViT) and a text encoder (transformer); 400M (image, caption) pairs collected from the web; **contrastive** learning (InfoNCE) on massive batches (up to 32k pairs).
:::

::: thm
[Contrastive loss: derivation]{.tag} In a batch of $N$ pairs $(v_i, t_i)$ (images and texts encoded and normalized), we compute the similarity matrix $S_{ij} = \langle v_i, t_j\rangle / \tau$ ($\tau$ the temperature). The symmetric InfoNCE loss: $$\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Big[\log\frac{e^{S_{ii}}}{\sum_j e^{S_{ij}}} + \log\frac{e^{S_{ii}}}{\sum_j e^{S_{ji}}}\Big].$$ Each term is a cross-entropy: in the *image→text direction*, classifying the right caption among $N$ candidates; in the *text→image direction*, the right image among $N$ — two crossed softmaxes on the same matrix.
:::

::: proof
Where does this form come from? Let $p_i(j) = \mathrm{softmax}(S_{i\cdot})_j$ denote the "which caption for image $i$" distribution. The first term is $-\log p_i(i)$: maximize the probability of the correct match. Expanding, $$-\log p_i(i) = -S_{ii} + \log\sum_j e^{S_{ij}} \;\ge\; -S_{ii} + \log e^{S_{ii}} = 0,$$ with equality iff the diagonal dominates its whole row: the loss pushes positive pairs up *and* the $N-1$ negatives down (softmax = a softmax competition of similarities). Link with mutual information (Oord et al., 2018): for negatives drawn from the product law, one can show the bound $$I(v; t) \;\ge\; \log N - \mathcal{L}_N,$$ where $I$ is the mutual information between modalities: InfoNCE maximizes a lower bound on $I$, ever tighter as $N$ grows — hence the value of giant batches (complete proof: NLP module, chapter on contrastive representations). [∎]{.qed}
:::

::: note
[Temperature]{.tag} $\tau$ (learned, initialized at 0.07) rescales the logits before the softmax: small $\tau$ = peaked distribution = gradient concentrated on the hardest negatives; large $\tau$ = uniform gradients (exercise 11). The same parameter appears in LLMs (M2 module) — same role: dosing the "severity" of the competition.
:::

::: prop
[Zero-shot classification: worked example]{.tag} No more fixed classification heads: the classes *become texts*. To classify an image among $K$ labels $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_K$: $$\hat k = \arg\max_k\ \big\langle v,\ t(\text{"a photo of a }\ell_k\text{"})\big\rangle.$$ *Numerical example.* Assume a 3-dimensional space, three classes {dog, cat, graph} and the normalized text embeddings $t_{\mathrm{dog}} = (0.8;\ 0.6;\ 0)$, $t_{\mathrm{cat}} = (0.6;\ 0.8;\ 0)$, $t_{\mathrm{graph}} = (0;\ 0;\ 1)$. For an image $v = (0.7;\ 0.5;\ 0.5)$: dot products $0.56 + 0.30 = 0.86$; $0.42 + 0.40 = 0.82$; $0.5$. Dog wins (argmax) — without any classifier ever having been trained on these classes: the transfer happens through language. Enriched prompts ("a photo of a $\ell$, a type of pet") act as a textual prior that refines the position of the prototypes.
:::

::: note
[CLIP, the multimodal Swiss Army knife]{.tag} CLIP is used everywhere: the text encoder of diffusion models; a similarity judge (R-Precision); image-text retrieval; moderation. **CLIPScore** for text-image alignment: $w\cdot\max(\cos(v, t), 0)$ with $w = 2.5$ (calibrated on human judgments; above \~0.3, the caption "sticks" to the image). **ImageBind** (sketch): aligning six modalities (image, text, audio, depth, thermal, IMU) *with the image as the pivot*: each modality is contrasted with the image only, and by the transitivity of the shared space, audio ↔ text emerge without ever having been paired. The bridge with the master's program: one can also align *graphs* and text in a common space (GNN ↔ LLM embeddings, Graph ML ch. 8) — the graph "modality" enters the same contrastive alignment machinery.
:::

```python
from PIL import Image
from transformers import CLIPProcessor, CLIPModel
import torch

model = CLIPModel.from_pretrained("openai/clip-vit-base-patch32")
proc  = CLIPProcessor.from_pretrained("openai/clip-vit-base-patch32")

img = Image.open("graphe.png")
texts = ["a graph drawing", "a cat", "a molecule", "a city map"]
inputs = proc(text=texts, images=img, return_tensors="pt", padding=True)
with torch.no_grad():
    out = model(**inputs)
probs = out.logits_per_image.softmax(dim=1)   # zero-shot classification
print(dict(zip(texts, probs[0].tolist())))

# InfoNCE loss "by hand" (batch of aligned pairs):
# logits = v_norm @ t_norm.T / tau ; targets = arange(N)
# loss = 0.5 * (CE(logits, tgt) + CE(logits.T, tgt))
```

## 6. Text-to-image: the complete pipeline {#ch6}

::: thm
[Architecture 6.1 — From sentence to pixel]{.tag} The industrial pipeline of a latent text-to-image generator:

  Step                   Component                        Role / details
  ---------------------- -------------------------------- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  1\. Tokenization       BPE / SentencePiece              prompt → token sequence (NLP module); truncated to 77–225 depending on the model
  2\. Text encoding      CLIP text encoder + T5/ByT5      tokens → $(L \times d)$ tensor; CLIP's pooled embedding also conditions adaLN (DiT)
  3\. Latent diffusion   U-Net or DiT + cross-attention   noise → denoised latent (20–50 steps, solver of ch. 4, CFG $\tilde\epsilon$)
  4\. Decoding           VAE decoder                      latent $(64\times64)$ → image $(512\times512)$ in a single pass
  5\. Refinement         refiner / super-resolution       ×2–4 upsampling (by diffusion at higher resolution or a super-resolution GAN — ch. 2)

Training the large models often *freezes* the text encoder and the VAE, learning only the denoiser; **LoRA** (Low-Rank Adaptation) even freezes the denoiser and learns only low-rank corrections in the cross-attention weights — the "domestic" thematic fine-tuning (a few dozen images, a few GPU-minutes).
:::

-   **Prompt engineering, quantitatively**: the prompt is a *gradient* on the conditioning: adding "photorealistic, 85 mm" shifts the embeddings and hence every CFG step. Measurable effects: position (the first tokens weigh more), saturation (beyond \~50 effective tokens, diminishing returns), *syntactic weighting* "(word:1.3)" = rescaling of the attention logit during inference training;
-   **Negative prompt**: the generalized version of CFG with two conditions — $\varnothing$ is replaced by $c_-$: $$\tilde\epsilon = \epsilon_\theta(x_t,t,c_-) + w\big(\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t,c_+) - \epsilon_\theta(x_t,t,c_-)\big),$$ the negative direction is *repelled* (thm. 4.1): "blurry, watermark, extra fingers";
-   **Seeds**: the seed fixes $x_T$ (and the solver's randomness); same seed + same prompt = same image under deterministic DDIM; one sweeps the seeds to pick the best realization before refining the prompt — the actual workflow of practitioners;
-   **Inference cost**: (number of steps) × (denoiser cost) + decoding; latency governs the industrial choice (fast solvers, 1-step distillation when diversity matters less).

## 7. Beyond images: video, 3D, multimodal LLMs {#ch7}

-   **Video**: *spatio-temporal* latents (the VAE compresses time as well: 2–4 frames per latent token), the denoiser interleaves *spatial attention* (intra-frame) and *temporal attention* (inter-frames); cost grows like (frames × resolution²), hence the cascades (low resolution → temporal upsampling); camera control and long-horizon coherence: open problems (cf. ch. 9, AKiRa);
-   **Captioning / VQA**: image encoder (ViT) + text decoder (transformer); trained on pairs; graphical VQA ("what is the shortest path?") — visual reasoning;
-   **Multimodal LLMs**: how to make an LLM "see"?
    -   **Linear projector** (LLaVA): $h_v = W\,p_i + b$ on each ViT patch — the image "words" are projected into the LLM's embedding space: simple, effective, lots of tokens;
    -   **Q-Former** (BLIP-2): 32 *learned* query vectors that cross-attend to the image features and produce 32 embeddings — a compact "visual summary"; freezes the LLM while pretraining the bridge;
    -   **Two-stage training protocol**: (1) *alignment pretraining* on immense (image, caption) corpora — learning the correspondence; (2) multimodal *instruction tuning* — conversations, reasoning, answering;
    -   **Audio**: discrete tokens of spectrograms or signals (neural codec) injected in the same way — same pattern, another modality (M2 module for the rest);
-   **3D**: NeRF (sketch): an MLP $(x, d) \mapsto (\sigma, c)$ (density, color) is optimized by differentiable *volume rendering*: $$C(r) = \int_{t_n}^{t_f} T(t)\,\sigma\big(r(t)\big)\,c\big(r(t), d\big)\,dt, \qquad T(t) = \exp\!\Big(-\!\int_{t_n}^{t}\sigma\big(r(s)\big)ds\Big),$$ that is, "the opacity accumulated along the ray weights the colors"; recent 3D generative models prefer **diffusion over point clouds and meshes** — discretization, operators, correspondence: this is exactly the syllabus of the M2 Geometric Deep Learning module (direct link);
-   **World models**: *action-conditioned* generation of interactive videos (learned simulators; link with the RL module, latent world; mention of Genie/Sora-like systems);
-   **Generative structured data**: text-to-graph (generating the schema of a network), graph-to-text (a report from a knowledge graph) — the exact intersection of the Graph ML and NLP modules;
-   **Multimodal agents**: perceiving (screenshot) and acting (click, code) — GUI agents combine vision + LLM + tools (RL module, ch. 7).

## 8. Evaluation, costs, ethics {#ch8}

::: thm
[Panel of metrics]{.tag}

  Metric          Measures                                                    Known limits
  --------------- ----------------------------------------------------------- -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  FID             distributional distance (W2/Bures on Inception features)    sampling bias (underestimated at small N — always compare at equal N), sensitive to the feature backbone, blind to text
  CLIPScore       prompt-image alignment (cosine)                             CLIP feature set; rewards clichés that are easy to describe
  LPIPS           diversity / perceptual similarity between generated pairs   judge network trained on limited human judgment
  IS              quality × diversity (classifier KL)                         sensitive to the classifier's dominant class
  Human studies   pairwise preferences (Elo)                                  costly, annotator biases — the final standard

The FID inherits the geometry of $W_2$ (OT module): the part $\mathrm{tr}\big(\Sigma_r + \Sigma_g - 2(\Sigma_r\Sigma_g)^{1/2}\big)$ is the *Bures distance* between covariances. Two practical pitfalls: (i) the number of samples — FID mechanically decreases with the cohort size; (ii) the features — InceptionV3 vs CLIP sometimes reorder the rankings. Always report (backbone, N, protocol).
:::

-   **Costs**: diffusion training = thousands of GPU-hours; inference = N denoiser steps + decoding; the quality/latency trade-off governs the industrial choice (fast solvers, distillation, quantization);
-   **Ethics — a balanced note**:
    -   *Deepfakes*: detectors (including detectors *using diffusion itself*), provenance;
    -   *Watermarking and provenance*: C2PA signed metadata (an industrial coalition: camera → editor → publication), invisible watermarks robust to re-compression — none is infallible alone, defense in depth;
    -   *Copyright*: training on web data — ongoing legal debates (opt-out, dataset licenses, filtering); on the generation side: similarity with training works must be monitored;
    -   *Bias*: corpus biases (representation, stereotypes) reappear amplified at generation — output audits, data documentation;
    -   *European AI Act*: a risk-tiered approach; synthetic generators are targeted there via transparency (marking of generated content, model documentation) — in connection with the M2 ethics seminar.

::: ex
[Project]{.tag} Complete pipeline: light fine-tuning of a latent diffusion model on a small thematic set (LoRA on cross-attention), with parameterizable CFG; evaluate FID/CLIPScore before/after and analyze the effect of the guidance weight $w$ (and of schedules $w(t)$ — cf. ch. 9).
:::

## 9. Course research notes (Kalogeiton et al.) {#ch9}

Vicky Kalogeiton (CVLab — École Polytechnique / ECL; formerly Inria Grenoble, LEAR team) has worked since her PhD on a coherent program: *localizing and understanding objects and actions in videos*, and more recently, *generating them*. The three publications below exactly mark out the syllabus of this course — with video as the common thread.

::: thm
[ACT-detector — Action Tubelet Detector (ICCV 2017)]{.tag} [arXiv:1705.01861](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.01861) — V. Kalogeiton, P. Weinzaepfel, V. Ferrari, C. Schmid. **Problem.** Spatio-temporal action detection: for each actor, find *where* (per-frame boxes) and *when* (temporal segment) each action is performed. **Method.** Extending anchor-based detection (SSD) to the spatio-temporal domain: the input is a *tubelet* — k consecutive frames — and the network regresses and scores 3D *cuboid-anchors* (position, spatial scale, duration), with oversampling of frame-level features for small actors. **Results.** State of the art at the time on UCF-Sports, J-HMDB and UCF101; the tubelet formalism fed the AVA benchmark. **Position in the course.** This is the "before" of transformers: 3D convolution + anchors, while chapters 3–4 of this module describe the "after" (DiT); the notion of *temporal scale* (pyramid of durations) foreshadows the temporal pyramid of modern video-to-text models.
:::

::: thm
[Analysis of Classifier-Free Guidance Weight Schedulers (TMLR 2024)]{.tag} [arXiv:2404.13040](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13040) — CVLab team. **Problem.** The guidance weight $w$ of thm. 4.1 is *constant* in most tools — why not vary it during sampling? **Method.** Systematic analysis of schedules $w(t)$ (increasing, decreasing, bell-shaped) on text-to-image diffusion, with fidelity (CLIPScore) and diversity measurements. **Results.** Variable $w(t)$ profiles improve the fidelity/diversity trade-off compared to constant $w$; the behavior depends on the step (start vs end of the chain). **Position.** Theorem 4.1 gives the theory of CFG at fixed $w$; this work shows that the *temporal degree of freedom* is underexploited — a textbook example of "fine engineering of a generative hyperparameter", and a direct topic for the project of ch. 8.
:::

::: thm
[Generating video: AKiRa and Di[M]o distillation (2024–2025)]{.tag} AKiRa — [arXiv:2412.14158](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.14158) (CVPR 2025) and Di[M]o — [arXiv:2503.15457](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.15457) (ICCV 2025). **AKiRa** (Augmentation Kit on Rays): an augmentation *kit* for optical video generation — camera on rays, multi-view consistency; the camera-control question (ch. 7) handled on the training side. **Di[M]o**: distilling a *masked* diffusion model into a *one-step* generator — the acceleration of ch. 4 pushed to the extreme (MDM → one-step generator). **Position.** The two ends of the value chain: quality/consistency (AKiRa) and latency (Di[M]o) — exactly the two axes of the industrial trade-off of ch. 8. Let us also mention [Don't drop your samples!](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.20324) (CVPR 2024): a *consistency* loss that improves the training of conditional diffusion models — the field diagnosis of the pathologies of ch. 3.
:::

::: note
[The common thread]{.tag} Perceiving video (detection, 2017) → generating it (video diffusion, 2024–2025) → accelerating it (distillation): the CVLab research trajectory mirrors that of the field — and that of this course, from GANs (ch. 2) to guided latent diffusion (ch. 4) up to complete systems (ch. 6).
:::

## Exercises {#ex}

1.  **Composition of noises.** Show by induction that $q(x_t \mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t} x_0, (1-\bar\alpha_t) I)$; why does this closed form make training efficient?
2.  **DDPM ELBO.** Decompose the log-likelihood $\log p_\theta(x_0)$ into per-step terms and show that the noise MSE dominates (the KLs between Gaussians are closed-form).
3.  **KL of Gaussians.** Prove proposition 0.4 in the scalar case by computing $\mathbb{E}_q[\log q - \log p]$; check that the KL is zero iff $\mu_1 = \mu_2, \sigma_1 = \sigma_2$ and strictly positive otherwise.
4.  **Mode collapse.** Simulate a 2D Gaussian→ring GAN; observe the collapse; compare with a diffusion model trained on the same set (diversity via LPIPS).
5.  **CFG.** Show that $w = 1$ recovers the conditional prediction and $w = 0$ the unconditional one; generate a grid $w \in \{0, 1, 5, 10\}$ and comment on the trade-off.
6.  **CLIP zero-shot.** Measure the zero-shot accuracy of a fine-tuned CLIP vs a ResNet trained on 10 custom classes as a function of training size; where do the curves cross?
7.  **FID and Wasserstein.** Recall the formula for $W_2^2$ between Gaussians (OT module) and show that the FID is an estimate of it (features; sampling bias).
8.  **Epsilon or score?** Using $x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon$, show that $\epsilon = -\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\nabla_{x_t}\log p(x_t \mid x_0)$.
9.  **Noise vs mean.** Parameterize the denoiser as predicting $x_0$ ($\hat x_0 = x_\theta(x_t, t)$); express the corresponding loss and explain when this parameterization is preferable (small $t$, vivid colors).
10. **Truncation.** For a StyleGAN whose $w$ approximately follows a centered Gaussian, show that the rule $w' = \bar w + \psi(w - \bar w)$, $\psi \in [0,1]$, reduces the variance of the generated style and comment on the quality/diversity trade-off as $\psi \to 0$.
11. **InfoNCE temperature.** In the contrastive loss of ch. 5, show the effect of $\tau \to 0$ (peaked distribution, gradients concentrated on the hardest negatives) and of $\tau \to \infty$ (uniform gradients, slowed learning).
12. **Project.** Complete pipeline: light fine-tuning of a latent diffusion model on a small thematic set (LoRA on cross-attention), with parameterizable CFG; evaluate FID/CLIPScore before/after and analyze the effect of the guidance weight $w$ — also testing variable schedules $w(t)$ (cf. ch. 9).

::: note
[Solution 1 — Composition of noises]{.tag} Induction: true at $t=1$ by definition; if $x_{t-1}\mid x_0$ is Gaussian with mean $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}x_0$ and variance $(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})I$, then $x_t = \sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1} + \sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\,\epsilon$ with $\epsilon$ independent; prop. 0.1 (sum of independent Gaussians) gives mean $\sqrt{\alpha_t\bar\alpha_{t-1}}x_0 = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0$ and variance $\alpha_t(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}) + (1-\alpha_t) = 1-\bar\alpha_t$. The closed form makes training efficient because the first $t-1$ steps are skipped: direct noising at any $t$, a single forward pass per training example.
:::

::: note
[Solution 2 — DDPM ELBO (plan)]{.tag} (1) Write the ELBO of the chain $p_\theta(x_{0:T})$ against $q$ and telescope (Markov chain): $L = L_T + \sum_t L_{t-1}$ with $L_{t-1} = \mathrm{KL}(q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)\,\|\,p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t))$. (2) $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t,x_0)$ is Gaussian (product of two Gaussians: Bayes + completing the square). (3) Every $L_{t-1}$ is a KL of Gaussians: closed (prop. 0.4); with $\sigma_t^2 = \tilde\beta_t$ there remains the gap between the means $\propto \|\tilde\mu_t - \mu_\theta\|^2$. (4) The parameterization $\mu_\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}(x_t - \frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\epsilon_\theta)$ exchanges the gap between means for the noise MSE — full details in the proof of model 3.2.
:::

::: note
[Solution 3 — KL of Gaussians (scalar case)]{.tag} $\mathrm{KL} = \mathbb{E}_q[\log q - \log p]$ with $\log q(x) = -\frac12\log(2\pi\sigma_1^2) - \frac{(x-\mu_1)^2}{2\sigma_1^2}$ and likewise for $p$. Difference: $\log q - \log p = \frac12\log\frac{\sigma_2^2}{\sigma_1^2} - \frac{(x-\mu_1)^2}{2\sigma_1^2} + \frac{(x-\mu_2)^2}{2\sigma_2^2}$. Now $\mathbb{E}_q[(x-\mu_1)^2] = \sigma_1^2$ and $\mathbb{E}_q[(x-\mu_2)^2] = \mathbb{E}[((x-\mu_1) + (\mu_1-\mu_2))^2] = \sigma_1^2 + (\mu_1-\mu_2)^2$ (zero cross term). Hence $\mathrm{KL}(q\|p) = \frac12\big[\log\frac{\sigma_2^2}{\sigma_1^2} + \frac{\sigma_1^2 + (\mu_1-\mu_2)^2}{\sigma_2^2} - 1\big]$. This is $\frac12[u - 1 - \log u] \ge 0$ with $u = \sigma_2^2/\sigma_1^2$ (since $\log u \le u - 1$) plus a squared term: zero iff $(\mu_1,\sigma_1) = (\mu_2,\sigma_2)$.
:::

::: note
[Solution 4 — 2D mini-GAN (code)]{.tag}

```python
import torch
G = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(2, 64), torch.nn.ReLU(),
                        torch.nn.Linear(64, 64), torch.nn.ReLU(),
                        torch.nn.Linear(64, 2))          # noise -> 2D point
D = torch.nn.Sequential(torch.nn.Linear(2, 64), torch.nn.ReLU(),
                        torch.nn.Linear(64, 1))          # point -> logit

def sample_ring(n, r=1.0, noise=.05):                    # true law: a ring
    a = torch.rand(n) * 2 * torch.pi
    return torch.stack([r*torch.cos(a), r*torch.sin(a)], 1) + noise*torch.randn(n, 2)

optG, optD = torch.optim.Adam(G.parameters(), 2e-4), torch.optim.Adam(D.parameters(), 2e-4)
bce = torch.nn.functional.binary_cross_entropy_with_logits
for step in range(5000):
    x = sample_ring(256); z = torch.randn(256, 2)
    lossD = bce(D(x), torch.ones(256, 1)) + bce(D(G(z)), torch.zeros(256, 1))
    optD.zero_grad(); lossD.backward(); optD.step()
    z = torch.randn(256, 2)
    lossG = bce(D(G(z)), torch.ones(256, 1))             # non-saturated form
    optG.zero_grad(); lossG.backward(); optG.step()
    if step % 1000 == 0: print(step, float(lossD), float(lossG))
# Observe: G concentrates on an arc of the circle (mode collapse);
# measure diversity: average distance between generated pairs.
```

The collapse is visible when the covered arc shrinks; compare with a 2D diffusion (same network for $\epsilon_\theta$): the denoising MSE covers the whole ring.
:::

::: note
[Solution 5 — CFG]{.tag} $\tilde\epsilon = \epsilon_\theta(\varnothing) + w(\epsilon_\theta(c) - \epsilon_\theta(\varnothing))$: for $w = 0$, $\tilde\epsilon = \epsilon_\theta(\varnothing)$ (unconditional); for $w = 1$, $\tilde\epsilon = \epsilon_\theta(c)$ (conditional). For $w > 1$, the proof of thm. 4.1 shows that $\tilde\epsilon$ is the score of $p(x\mid c)^w p(x)^{1-w}$: an "over-weighted" conditional distribution, more peaked — increased prompt fidelity, reduced diversity (fewer samples explored). Typical grid: at $w=0$, off-topic images; $w=1$, correct and varied; $w=5$, highly compliant, repetitive; $w=10$, saturation (burnt colors, artifacts).
:::

::: note
[Solution 7 — FID and W2 (Bures)]{.tag} For two Gaussians $\mathcal{N}(\mu_1,\Sigma_1)$, $\mathcal{N}(\mu_2,\Sigma_2)$: $$W_2^2 = \|\mu_1 - \mu_2\|^2 + \mathrm{tr}\big(\Sigma_1 + \Sigma_2 - 2(\Sigma_1^{1/2}\Sigma_2\Sigma_1^{1/2})^{1/2}\big)$$ (proof: the diagonal case by rotation, then the general one — OT module). The FID is exactly this formula applied to the Gaussians *fitted to the Inception features* of the two image sets — an approximation of $W_2$ both through the features (transport happens only in the backbone's space) and through the moment estimates ($\hat\mu, \hat\Sigma$ on N samples: the FID is *biased downward* at small N — always compare at equal cohort size).
:::

::: note
[Solution 8 — Epsilon = -sqrt(1-a_bar) x score]{.tag} See the proof of theorem 3.3: for $p(x_t\mid x_0) = \mathcal{N}(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0, (1-\bar\alpha_t)I)$, $\nabla_{x_t}\log p = -(x_t - \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0)/(1-\bar\alpha_t) = -\epsilon/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}$, hence $\epsilon = -\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\nabla_{x_t}\log p(x_t\mid x_0)$. Consequence: the denoising MSE is a regression onto the conditional score; integrating over $x_0$, it targets the marginal score $\nabla\log p_t(x_t)$ — the starting point of the SDE formulation (ch. 4).
:::
